newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain announces sweeping privatisation drive.
newsitem.headline: Spain announces sweeping privatisation drive.

text.p: Spain on Monday unveiled an aggressive drive to raise privatisation earnings with plans to sell off its remaining stakes in three companies and part of a fourth.

The government plans to sell next year its last 21.2 percent holding in telephone operator Telefonica, 25 percent of banking group Argentaria and 10 percent of Repsol. It also plans to sell part of its 66 percent holding in electricity group Endesa.

"The placement of Telefonica is being considered for the beginning of the year. Repsol is seen for the spring," a spokesman for the Industry Ministry told Reuters, commenting on statements made by Industry Minister Josep Pique in Barcelona.
The punishing schedule -- together with plans to sell stakes this year in Gas Natural, Enagas, Auxini, Muxini and Aldeasa -- could overstretch the market's appetite, analysts said.

"I don't know if international markets have room enough to buy all this. It seems to me more likely they plan to do it in three years' time," said Jose Manuel Castellano at Banco Bilbao Vizcaya Interactivos.
But although the pace of planned sales is fast, some analysts said they believed the government could manage it.

"They can do it if we judge from successes they had in previous privatisations. It is true this is going to be a lot of paper for the market but they can stick to a schedule like this," said Javier Borrachero, analyst at Banco Central Hispano.

In July, Spain said it expected to earn some 600 billion pesetas ($4.66 billion) from privatisations in 1997. But in its budget draft presented last month, the government opted for a more conservative estimate of 450 billion pesetas.

"On the budget they forecast 450 billion pesetas from the privatisation process and if they really sell it all -- they won't have very much left if they do -- then they can make more than one trillion pesetas," Castellano said.

The huge sale would leave the five-month-old government, which is eager to ensure it will narrow its deficit to exacting European standards next year, with few plums left to sell other than Endesa, Tabacalera and Retevision.

Although the conservative-led government was clearly in a rush, the international appeal of Telefonica should make its sale a success despite the heavy competition from other international flotations at the same time, one analyst said.
"Telefonica is very popular outside Spain. It is the most liquid stock we have. The competition is strong."
Germany's Deutsche Telekom is due to come to market next month, Italy's STET in March and France Telecom's turn comes in April.
"That's why they have to do it fast, to be ready at the beginning of 1997, but I still think Telefonica is appealing," Borrachero said. ($1=128.7 Peseta)
